# Muscatine Mall

The Muscatine Mall, located in Muscatine, Iowa, stands as a significant example of American retail architecture and commerce, reflecting the profound transformations experienced by regional malls across the United States over the past five decades. Originally opened in 1971 as Muscatine Plaza, it served as a central hub for commerce and social activity in the Quad-Cities area , . Its history encapsulates key industry shifts, including the rise of big-box retail, the consolidation of department store chains, and the increasing obsolescence of single-screen movie theaters. Over the years, the mall has undergone multiple ownership changes, witnessed the departure of numerous anchor tenants, and faced periods of significant vacancy. However, as of late 2025, the property is undergoing a strategic transformation, pivoting from a purely transactional commercial space toward a multifunctional community venue and a potential site for mixed-use residential development. This evolution highlights an adaptive response to a changing economic landscape, attempting to redefine its role within the community amidst ongoing challenges related to competition and shifting consumer habits. The mall's journey serves as a microcosm of the broader narrative of American retail, illustrating both the resilience and the profound structural changes required for survival in the modern era.

## Founding and Early Development

The origins of the Muscatine Mall trace back to the early 1970s, a period characterized by rapid suburban expansion and the growth of large-scale enclosed shopping centers designed to become primary destinations for regional consumers. The property, initially named Muscatine Plaza, opened its doors in 1971 , . It was developed by General Management, a company that envisioned the plaza not merely as a collection of individual stores but as an integrated commercial and entertainment complex . This holistic approach was reflected in its initial tenant mix, which featured two prominent anchor stores: Woolworth and Montgomery Ward . These anchors were typical of the era and represented leading national retail brands, providing a strong draw for shoppers from Muscatine and surrounding communities. The inclusion of entertainment from its inception was a deliberate strategy to enhance its appeal. On July 23, 1971, the Plaza Twin Theatre opened alongside the shopping center, operated by the L&M Circuit as an 850-seat cinema . The construction of this theater was announced in Boxoffice magazine as part of a larger plan by developer Matthew Buckshaum to include four such theaters in his Iowa shopping centers, underscoring the vision of creating a destination-oriented environment where families could shop and be entertained under one roof .

The early years of the mall's operation solidified its position as a dominant retail force in the region. In 1975, the mall underwent a significant expansion with the addition of JCPenney as a third anchor store, further strengthening its appeal and broadening its product offerings . This period represents the zenith of the traditional regional mall model, where a curated selection of national department stores and specialty shops created a captive audience. The presence of three major anchors—Woolworth, Montgomery Ward, and JCPenney—provided a powerful combination of variety and scale, attracting substantial foot traffic. The development was strategically positioned to capture the growing population and economic activity in Muscatine during that decade. The acquisition of the property by Aetna Life Insurance and The Rouse Company in 1980 for $91 million signaled its perceived value and importance in the regional real estate market . This sale was part of a larger portfolio transaction involving ten malls, six of which were located in Iowa, highlighting the geographic concentration of such developments and the significance of Muscatine Plaza within that network . The purchase by General Growth Properties (the successor to Rouse Companies) underscored the asset's status as a key component of a valuable retail portfolio. The early development phase established the physical and functional framework of the mall, defining its identity as a cornerstone of local commerce and a vital piece of the community's infrastructure for nearly a quarter-century. The foundational choices made during this period—including the selection of anchors and the integration of a cinema—would have lasting consequences, shaping the property's trajectory through decades of economic and cultural change.

## Anchor Tenant Evolution and Competitive Shifts

The history of the Muscatine Mall is intrinsically linked to the story of its anchor tenants, whose arrivals and departures chart the course of its fortunes. The original trio of Woolworth, Montgomery Ward, and JCPenney formed the bedrock of its success in the 1970s and early 1980s . However, the competitive landscape began to shift dramatically in the mid-to-late 1980s. A pivotal moment occurred around 1987 when a new competitor entered the market: Wal-Mart relocated its downtown Muscatine store into the mall as an anchor tenant . While intended to attract a broader customer base, the presence of a massive discount retailer directly competing with the existing department stores fundamentally altered the dynamics of the enclosed shopping center. This move marked the beginning of a trend where off-mall competitors would challenge the very viability of the traditional mall model. The situation escalated when, around 1997, this same Wal-Mart relocated again, this time to a new standalone SuperCenter along the US 61 bypass . This "anchor migration" was a significant blow, as it removed a major draw from the interior of the mall while simultaneously freeing up a prime anchor space that would become a revolving door for subsequent tenants.

Following the departure of the first Wal-Mart, the south anchor spot saw a flurry of activity. Von Maur briefly took occupancy in 1995 but left shortly thereafter . Staples moved in next, occupying the space for approximately two years before closing in early 2002 . Concurrently, the original Woolworth store had been converted to Woolco in 1983, which itself closed in 1983, leaving behind a void that was eventually filled by Iowa's first Walmart before its relocation . The former Montgomery Ward anchor also experienced a series of transitions, evolving through Von Maur and Staples before being replaced by Elder-Beerman in late 2003 , . This period of intense volatility among the remaining anchors highlighted the mall's struggle to secure stable, long-term tenants capable of drawing consistent crowds. The eventual acquisition of the mall by Chicago-based Landau & Heyman in August 1998, as part of a multi-mall buyout, brought a new management philosophy focused on providing quality shopping in under-served markets and adding value through improvements . Despite this new focus, the anchor instability continued. Elder-Beerman became a more permanent fixture, but the space previously occupied by Staples was later taken by Younkers, which had evolved from Compton's Furniture & More, before finally becoming Warehouse Bargains . Meanwhile, the east end of the mall saw the arrival of Menards, which replaced Wal-Mart's north anchor spot around 1998 . Menards' presence was notable, but its entrance was eventually sealed, and the interior corridor connecting it to JCPenney was cordoned off, signaling a decline in the mall's connectivity and vibrancy .

The final decades of the mall's tenure as a traditional shopping center were defined by the loss of its last two major department store anchors, a double blow that effectively dismantled its ability to function as a regional retail hub. JCPenney, one of the original anchors, closed its Muscatine location in 2014 . Then, in August 2018, the closure of Younkers marked the end of another iconic regional institution. Younkers was a significant part of Iowa's retail heritage, founded in Keokuk in 1856 and having operated seventeen stores across the state prior to its parent company, Bon-Ton Stores Inc., filing for bankruptcy . The liquidation of the chain eliminated a key anchor presence in multiple Iowa malls and represented a significant loss for the Muscatine community . These departures stripped the mall of its primary draw, leaving behind a shell with a diminished tenant mix. By late 2024 and early 2025, the mall was reported to remain approximately half-vacant, confirming its precarious state . The constant pressure from off-mall competitors, coupled with the relentless churn in anchor tenants, illustrates the immense challenges faced by the mall in adapting to a rapidly evolving retail environment dominated by e-commerce and big-box formats.

## Period of Decline and Vacancy

Following the closures of its final two major department store anchors, JCPenney in 2014 and Younkers in 2018, the Muscatine Mall entered a prolonged period of decline and significant vacancy , . The departure of these establishments removed the last vestiges of the mall's traditional function as a regional shopping center, leaving behind a vast amount of empty space and a greatly diminished tenant roster. By late 2024 and early 2025, the mall was described as being approximately half-vacant, indicating that despite some efforts at revitalization, its core business model had largely failed . The physical condition of the mall deteriorated during this period; the interior corridor between Menards and JCPenney, once a bustling shopping thoroughfare, was sealed off and labeled "closed for maintenance" as early as November 2005, foreshadowing the larger issues of decay to come . The mall's struggles were exacerbated by its unique geographic position, situated between the larger metropolitan areas of Davenport and Iowa City . Muscatine Mayor Dianna Broderson acknowledged this challenge, noting that the city has worked with the mall over the years to try to revitalize it, but that attracting large retailers to fill the void left by departing anchors has been a persistent difficulty .

Despite the overall decline, certain tenants managed to survive and even thrive, often occupying former anchor spaces or smaller kiosks. Slumberland Furniture, for instance, has maintained a continuous presence inside the mall, demonstrating the viability of specialized home goods retailers even in a struggling environment , . As of December 2025, Slumberland Muscatine is actively operating, offering a wide range of products from Ashley Furniture to La-Z-Boy and Tempur-Pedic, and providing services like in-store pickup and delivery to residents , . Another resilient tenant is JOANN Fabric, which operates alongside Slumberland, suggesting that craft and hobby-related businesses may have found a niche within the mall's structure . The food court area also remains active, housing businesses such as Hallmark Gold Crown, Hibbett Sports, China Buffet, ExpertTire, and a wireless store, all of which operate from exterior-access-only locations, a testament to the mall's adaptation to its reduced capacity . Additionally, a driver's license station was located within the mall, providing essential public services and contributing to the building's utility .

The mall's entertainment component, the Plaza Twin Theatre, also experienced a turbulent history. Initially opening in 1971 as part of the original shopping center, it expanded to four screens in 1993 and was renamed Plaza 4 Theatre . Operated by Fridley Theatres, it served as the only movie screens in Muscatine for many years . However, its tenure came to an end on May 4, 2013, after the opening of a new 10-screen multiplex in the area, which rendered the older, smaller theater obsolete . The closure of the theater was a significant event, removing another key attraction from the complex. Throughout this period of decline, the mall's management, particularly under the ownership group of Kevin Koellner, Scott Anderson, and Rod Blackwell, who acquired the property in July 2005, attempted to make repairs and improve the building's exterior , . However, these efforts appeared insufficient to halt the slide into vacancy. The overall atmosphere of the mall during this time was one of quiet desolation; as of Thanksgiving 2005, the interior corridors were largely vacant and nonfunctional, with only minor seasonal activations like a Santa Claus display near JCPenney breaking the stillness . This physical and commercial decay contributed to a negative feedback loop, where the lack of vibrant tenants deterred customers, which in turn made it harder to lease the remaining spaces, perpetuating the cycle of decline.

## Modern Revitalization and Community Integration

In late 2025, the Muscatine Mall is no longer just a relic of a bygone retail era but is actively engaged in a multifaceted revitalization effort aimed at re-establishing its relevance as a community asset. This modern phase of its existence is characterized by a dual strategy: short-term activation through community events and long-term planning for a fundamental transformation of the property's use. A key indicator of this renewed focus is the mall's hosting of the 'Handcrafted Christmas' indoor holiday market on Saturday, December 13, 2025 . This event, co-located with the Muscatine Area Farmers Market’s 'Handcrafted Christmas' indoor market, transformed the mall into a vibrant venue for local artisans and makers to sell handmade gifts, holiday décor, baked goods, and artisanal foods . Such events leverage the mall's central location and large, flexible interior space to create a temporary, festive atmosphere that draws foot traffic from the community. By partnering with local organizations like the Muscatine Area Farmers Market, the mall management is fostering collaboration and positioning the property as a platform for small businesses and creative entrepreneurs rather than solely a venue for large national chains . Other events, such as the 'Elves Workshop,' a free drop-in children's craft event featuring Santa and elves, further demonstrate this pivot towards community engagement and family-friendly programming .

This strategy of using the mall as a community hub is complemented by the continued presence and operational success of select retail tenants. Slumberland Furniture, as mentioned, remains a robust and active presence, serving as a testament to the viability of specialized retail niches within the mall's footprint , . Its sustained operations, complete with a strong online reputation (a 4.6-star Google rating) and a diverse product line including high-end mattress brands like Purple and Tempur-Pedic, indicate that the business has successfully adapted to the local market , . The fact that Slumberland continues to offer full-service delivery and in-store pickup suggests that it has built a loyal customer base that values its physical presence and services, even within a challenging retail environment . The persistence of these smaller, well-managed tenants provides a foundation upon which further revitalization efforts can be built. They contribute to a baseline level of activity and create pockets of vitality within the larger complex.

Furthermore, the mall's current owners, Muscatine Mall Management, LLC, appear to be driving these positive changes. Formed in 2005 by a group of locally based businessmen—Kevin Koellner, Scott Anderson, and Rod Blackwell—the firm has been managing the property since its acquisition , . Their local roots suggest a vested interest in the property's long-term success and a deeper understanding of the community's needs compared to previous absentee owners . Reports from 2025 mention that repairs have been made to the building's exterior and that further improvements are scheduled, indicating a commitment to maintaining and upgrading the physical infrastructure . The leadership team includes individuals with extensive local development experience, such as Scott Anderson, President of Cedar Development, and Kevin Koellner, President of Build to Suit Inc., who bring expertise in developing other successful commercial properties in the Quad-Cities area . This local knowledge and hands-on management style likely plays a crucial role in the mall's ability to adapt and respond to community needs. The combination of community-focused events, the support of thriving local tenants, and proactive management from a dedicated local owner group represents a concerted effort to breathe new life into the Muscatine Mall, transforming it from a symbol of decline into a dynamic and integral part of the fabric of Muscatine.

## Redevelopment Plans and Future Outlook

The future of the Muscatine Mall is being shaped by a visionary and ambitious plan for its redevelopment, which marks a fundamental departure from its original purpose as a shopping center. This long-term strategy is officially embedded within the city of Muscatine's updated Comprehensive Plan, titled 'Make It Muscatine: Comprehensive Plan 2025–2045' . The plan, developed in partnership with RDG Planning & Design, aims to guide land use, development, and investment in the city through 2045, and it explicitly identifies the Muscatine Mall as a key site for transformation . The proposal emerging from this process involves converting the mall property into a mixed-use area that would include housing units such as houses and apartments . This plan is not merely speculative; it originated directly from over 200 suggestions collected during a robust public engagement process conducted as part of the comprehensive plan update . The process involved collaboration with city staff, private businesses, and residents, culminating in a draft released in late 2024 and a public Design Studio held in January 2025, demonstrating a community-driven approach to the mall's future .

The rationale behind this transformative vision is rooted in contemporary urban planning principles that prioritize density, walkability, and mixed-use development over sprawling, car-dependent commercial zones. By converting the mall site into a residential neighborhood, the city aims to create a more vibrant, 24/7 community hub. This approach seeks to address the underlying causes of the mall's decline by integrating it into the urban fabric, making it a place people live, work, and play, rather than just a destination they visit for shopping. The redevelopment plan aligns with the four guiding themes of the comprehensive plan: 'Make it Ambitious', 'Make it Home', 'Make it Connected', and 'Make it Adventurous' . Transforming the mall into a residential area directly supports the 'Make it Home' theme, aiming to provide new housing options and increase the city's population density in a sustainable manner. This represents a pragmatic acceptance that the traditional retail model that supported the mall for decades is no longer viable and that a new economic and social function must be found for the valuable property.

While the redevelopment plan provides a compelling long-term vision, its implementation will face practical and financial hurdles. The transition from a commercial property to a residential one requires significant capital investment, zoning changes, and careful architectural planning. The success of the project will depend heavily on securing financing, navigating regulatory approvals, and building consensus among stakeholders, including residents, business owners, and investors. The involvement of the current local ownership group, Muscatine Mall Management, LLC, will be critical, as their willingness to partner with the city and potentially participate in the redevelopment will be a key factor in moving the plan forward . The mall's current state, with its existing structures and infrastructure, will present both opportunities and challenges for redevelopment. Some parts of the building may be repurposed or incorporated into new residential buildings, while others may need to be demolished to accommodate a new design. The outcome of this process will ultimately determine whether the Muscatine Mall can successfully reinvent itself, or if it will be completely reimagined and rebuilt to meet the needs of Muscatine's future. The debate between preserving its historical character versus embracing a radical new form of urban living is the central controversy shaping its destiny.

## Historical Context and Legacy

The Muscatine Mall occupies a unique place in the history of American retail, serving as a tangible representation of the nation's post-war economic boom, the rise of suburban culture, and the seismic shifts that have reshaped the commercial landscape in the 21st century. Opened in 1971, the mall embodies the peak of the regional shopping center model, a concept pioneered in the mid-20th century that sought to centralize retail activity and create self-contained communities of consumption , . Its original configuration—with anchors like JCPenney, Woolworth, and Montgomery Ward, plus an integrated theater—was designed to be a destination in itself, a place where families could spend an entire day , . For decades, it successfully fulfilled this role, becoming a cornerstone of Muscatine's economy and a familiar landmark for generations of residents. Its history is therefore not just a story of a single building, but a chronicle of how retail, consumerism, and community life have evolved over the past fifty years.

The legacy of the Muscatine Mall is one of both achievement and poignant decline. Its early success demonstrated the power of the enclosed mall model to generate wealth and foster a sense of shared community space. However, its subsequent struggles and near-vacancy highlight the vulnerabilities of this model in the face of technological disruption, changing consumer preferences, and the inexorable rise of e-commerce and big-box retail. The mall's story is a case study in competitive disruption, from the disruptive arrival of Wal-Mart in the 1980s to the eventual bankruptcy of department store giants like Bon-Ton, which led to the departure of anchors like Younkers , . The mall's fate underscores the geographic challenges faced by smaller-market retail properties, which often lack the scale and customer base to compete with larger metropolitan centers . Its journey reflects a broader national trend of "mall death," where many similar properties across the country have fallen into disrepair or been demolished.

Ultimately, the enduring legacy of the Muscatine Mall lies in its adaptability and its continued relevance to the community, albeit in new forms. Even in its most dilapidated state, the property was never entirely abandoned. The long-running presence of the Plaza Twin Theatre until 2013 provided a consistent draw, and the more recent use of the space for farmers markets and holiday fairs demonstrates its capacity to serve as a flexible venue for community activities , . The current push toward mixed-use redevelopment signifies a final, strategic pivot away from its original purpose, acknowledging that its greatest value now may lie not in its commercial capacity, but in its physical footprint and central location as a catalyst for urban renewal. The Muscatine Mall's story is thus a powerful reminder of the cyclical nature of urban development. It has weathered the storm of industrial change, and its future, whether as a revitalized community hub or a new residential neighborhood, ensures that its legacy will continue to shape the identity and growth of Muscatine for decades to come.

    ### [City offices closed Dec. 24-25; update on refuse, recycling schedule](https://www.muscatineiowa.gov/m/newsflash/Home/Detail/4958)

    *   Thursday’s route will be collected Friday and Friday’s route collected on Saturday.

    ### [Muscatine Police Chief Awarded Peer-Recognized Medal of Merit](https://www.muscatineiowa.gov/m/newsflash/Home/Detail/4955)
    
    **MUSCATINE, Iowa** – A third member of the Muscatine Police Department whose leadership and compassion have significantly strengthened public safety in Muscatine was recognized Tuesday (Dec. 16) with the Muscatine Police Department (MPD) Medal of Merit during the Muscatine City Council meeting.
    
    Police Chief Anthony Kies received the honor, joining Assistant Chief Steve Snider and Co-Responder Amy Gold as Medal of Merit recipients. Snider and Gold were recognized during the December 2 City Council meeting. Kies presented the awards to Snider and Gold at the Dec. 2 meeting.
    
    “What Chief Kies did not tell the City Council at that time was that he was also being honored with the award,” Snider said.
    
    Snider explained that the Medal of Merit is not granted by a single individual but is awarded only after a nomination is reviewed by a committee of peers and receives a unanimous vote.
    
    “This is truly an award given by one’s peers,” Snider said.
    
    According to Snider, Kies was nominated for his career-long accomplishments and his tireless efforts to strengthen the Muscatine Police Department as a whole. Kies joined MPD in 2005 and has overseen several key initiatives, including the Evidence Technician Program and the Tactical Response Team.
    
    Kies led the formation of the area’s first multi-jurisdictional tactical response team by combining the city and county units into a single team. Under his leadership, new equipment and technology were added to enhance training, skill development and response capabilities.
    
    “I brought him a crazy idea I had of escorting paramedics into a hot scene to immediately treat the wounded,” Snider said. “That conversation led to the development of the Rescue Task Force philosophy, which has been adopted by both the police and fire departments.”
    
    Snider added that Kies was instrumental in developing the training necessary to advance that philosophy. Kies also helped expand self-defense classes and run-hide-fight training opportunities to the community.
    
    “Most importantly, since taking over as chief, he has emphasized the importance of family, self-care, and mental wellness, while increasing access for people to take time off when they need it to be with their families,” Snider said. “That focus has rolled into a very happy department and a department that has seen a big reduction in turnover and a much higher retention than in the past.”
    
    Assistant Chief Steve Snider and Co-Responder Amy Gold were recognized December 2 for their exceptional service and leadership within the Muscatine Police Department. Snider was honored for his longstanding commitment to innovation, training, and officer safety, while Gold was recognized for her compassionate work through the co-responder program, strengthening partnerships between law enforcement and mental health services and improving outcomes for individuals in crisis.

    ### [City to reopen Compost Facility one final day](https://www.muscatineiowa.gov/m/newsflash/Home/Detail/4953)
    
    **MUSCATINE, Iowa** – Despite the winter weather and lingering snow, the City of Muscatine will reopen the Compost Facility for one final day before the winter break.
    
    “To give residents one last chance to dispose of leaves and other yard waste this season, the Compost Facility will be open this Saturday, December 13, from 9:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m.,” said David Popp, Solid Waste Manager. “This will be the last day the site is open until spring.”
    
    The facility has been closed since December 6 due to recent snowstorms, but the Muscatine Transfer Station has received calls from residents asking when it would reopen.
    
    “It seems many residents still have leaves they want to get rid of before winter fully sets in,” Popp said.
    
    **Curbside Yard Waste Collection Continues**
    
    Even with the Compost Facility’s temporary closure, curbside yard waste collection will continue on residents’ normal trash collection days. Residents can place bagged yard waste or bundled brush at the curb for pickup.
    
    _Guidelines for Curbside Yard Waste Collection:_
    
    *   Only grass clippings, leaves, and garden waste will be collected.
    *   Yard waste must be in 20- or 30-gallon paper bags with a City yard waste sticker.
    *   Bags should not exceed 50 lbs and should be kept dry.
    *   Stickers are for residential yard waste only.
    *   Place bags at the curb after 5 p.m. the day before collection but before 5 a.m. on collection day.
    *   City of Muscatine Yard Waste Stickers are available at:
        1.  Muscatine Transfer Station
        2.  City Hall
        3.  Public Works
        4.  Hy-Vee (both locations)
        5.  Fareway
    
    Residents are encouraged to take advantage of the final Compost Facility day or use the curbside collection service to manage yard waste before winter fully arrives.

    ### [Carver Corner update, Comprehensive Plan on Council agenda](https://www.muscatineiowa.gov/m/newsflash/Home/Detail/4954)
    
    **MUSCATINE, Iowa** – Reconstruction of the Hershey Avenue and Green Street connection between Mississippi Drive and Grandview Avenue will be one of four topics to be discussed during the Muscatine City Council’s monthly in-depth meeting scheduled for 5:30 p.m. Tuesday, December 9, in the City Council Chambers at Muscatine City Hall.
    
    **Carver Corner Construction Design Update**
    
    City of Muscatine Engineer Kevin Coon will lead the discussion and provide a design update for the intersection, commonly known as Carver Corner, that could become Muscatine’s third roundabout in 2026. This project represents the final phase of long-term improvements along the Business 61 corridor, stretching from the Highway 61 Bypass through the Downtown district.
    
    The Business 61 transformation began with the Mississippi Drive corridor project, started in 2017, and continued with the Grandview Avenue Corridor Project, started in 2022. These efforts have included the Mulberry-2nd Avenue roundabout, streetscape enhancements, and a sidewalk extension on Grandview Avenue from Houser Avenue south.
    
    **Comprehensive Plan 2025-2045**
    
    Community Development Director Jodi Royal-Goodwin will present the draft of Comprehensive Plan, 2025-2045, to the City Council. The plan outlines long-term goals for land use, zoning, economic development, transportation, housing, recreation, services, amenities, and public safety.
    
    Developed over more than a year with strong community input and data analysis, the plan replaces the 2013 version and reflects Muscatine’s recent growth and changing needs. Once adopted, it will guide land-use decisions and shape the city’s vision for the next decade and beyond.
    
    **City Council Goals Review**
    
    City Administrator Matt Mardesen will lead the final two agenda items, beginning with a review of the City Council’s annual goals. These goals support the City’s core values, vision, and mission, and help guide policy decisions and resource planning throughout the fiscal year.
    
    **Downtown Parking Evaluation**
    
    The meeting will conclude with an update on the City’s ongoing analysis of Downtown parking. Staff have been collecting data during the City’s free two-hour holiday parking period, which runs through January 4.
    
    **Public Participation Encouraged**
    
    All City Council meetings are open to the public, providing residents an opportunity to observe and participate in local government decision-making.
    
    Residents may attend in person at Muscatine City Hall, 215 Sycamore Street, or watch the meeting live on Civic-TV (MPW Channel 2) or the City of Muscatine YouTube channel.
    
    Meeting agendas and supporting documents are posted at least 24 hours in advance on the City’s website under Agenda & Minutes.
    
    Individuals requiring accommodations should contact the City Clerk’s Office at 563-264-1550 at least 24 hours before the meeting.
    
    For more information or to view the full agenda, visit the City’s website at muscatineiowa.gov.

MUSCATINE, Iowa — For Andrew Anderson, Muscatine will always be home. The real estate agent spent a few years in the Big Apple but said the glitz and glamour couldn't keep him away from Pearl of the Mississippi.

"We love our places that we live, both for what they are and also what the potential is. What they can be," the Muscatine native said.

Anderson returned just in time to help steer Muscatine for the next decade. [The city is updating its comprehensive plan](https://rdgusa.mysocialpinpoint.com/planmuscatine/plan-muscatine-page-1/), collaborating with the community on a roadmap for lawmakers and city developers. 82 goals were created under the previous plan, and development directors like Jodi Royal-Goodwin say progress was made in almost all of them.

"We celebrate the success we've had and where we've come from, but now, where do we want to go?" Royal-Goodwin said. "What's the next step? How do we make this the greatest place on Earth?"

She says residents have shared over 200 suggestions with dreams big and small. Some would like to turn the Muscatine Mall into a mixed use area to create additional houses and apartments. Others hope to straighten out some of the chaos on the streets asking for a round about at the intersection of East Fourth St. and Park Ave.

"Everybody ages and wants different things," Goodwin-Royal said. "We've made great progress, like you said, on the last comprehensive plan, but now, we get to have new input."

Anderson shares Royal-Goodwin's vision, and he thanked Wednesday's guests for their participation.

"Cities aren't just built by official city makers. They're built by a collaboration. It's the industry, the businesses, city and the residents," Anderson said.

RDG Planning and Design will take the feedback and revise its plans. Once they do that, RDG will present its new outlook to members of the steering committee, who will meet once a month.

Those who missed tonight's meeting can still submit ideas and suggestions [here](https://rdgusa.mysocialpinpoint.com/planmuscatine/planmuscatine_map#/).

MUSCATINE MALL: MUSCATINE, IA

* * *

Jason Hancock's Commentary
--------------------------

_Posted September 3, 2006 (user submitted December 6, 2005)_On the day before Thanksgiving, 2005, I took a detour from my trip from Des Moines to Davenport and stopped in Muscatine, a city of about 23,000 on the Mississippi River some 15 miles south of Interstate 80. I visited Muscatine Mall and was surprised to see how dead it was. It's anchored by JCPenney, Elder-Beerman (the only one in Iowa), and Menards, but there is little in between.

Muscatine Mall opened in 1971, but I don't know much else about the history of the mall. I remember a 1987 trip there as an 11-year-old because that was the first time I had ever visited a Wal-Mart, two years before the one in Davenport opened. In 1995, Muscatine Mall had Wal-Mart, JCPenney, and Von Maur as its anchors as well as Walgreens, B. Dalton, Foot Locker, Musicland, Radio Shack, and other typical mall stores, about 50 in all. Around 1997, though, Wal-Mart moved to a new SuperCenter along the US 61 bypass. Menards replaced Wal-Mart's north anchor spot about a year later. While it is certainly unusual to have a Menards in an enclosed shopping mall, as most of the home improvement chain's stores are free-standing, it's not unique: Marshall Town Center in Marshalltown, IA, also has one. Yet Menards has replaced many of its smaller stores with new, larger, free-standing stores in recent years, which has led to some speculation on the future of its Muscatine Mall store. Von Maur left the south anchor spot shortly after Wal-Mart left and Staples occupied it for about two years, but its early 2002 closing put the mall's future in jeopardy until Elder-Beerman replaced Staples in late 2003. Walgreens left the mall for a free-standing store just south of the mall shortly before Staples closed, and a lot of the smaller stores started closing around that time.

As of Thanksgiving 2005, the only chain stores left inside the mall are GNC and Regis Hairstylists. There are also the Plaza 4 Theaters (the only movie screens in Muscatine) and a handful of mom-and-pop stores, but there are only about 10 stores in the mall's interior aside from the anchors. Most of the interior corridor between Menards and JCPenney was "closed for maintenance," and Menards' mall entrance was sealed. Two stores -- a Hallmark Gold Crown shop and Hibbett Sports -- and a China Buffet have opened in the former Walgreens space but they have exterior entrances only, without access to the mall's interior. An ExpertTire store, an Iowa driver's license station, and a wireless store also have exterior entrances without mall access. On my Thanksgiving-eve visit, the only "shoppers" in the mall corridor appeared to be a bunch of teens hanging out by the theaters. There was also a Santa Claus display in the center of the mall near JCPenney, but that was it.

All this makes me wonder what caused the mall to go downhill. The nearest regional malls -- Northpark in Davenport, Southpark in Moline, and Coral Ridge in Coralville -- are 30-45 minutes away.

### \[ARCHIVED\] Draft of Comprehensive Plan 2025–2045 released; public input encouraged

![Image 3: Make it Muscatine Comprehensive Plan 2025-2045 DRAFT Cover (JPG)](http://muscatineiowa.gov/ImageRepository/Document?documentID=31523)

**MUSCATINE, Iowa** – The City of Muscatine is updating its Comprehensive Plan—an essential tool that will help guide future growth, development, and investment over the next 15 to 20 years. Originally adopted in 2013, the updated plan — **Make It Muscatine: Comprehensive Plan 2025–2045** — reflects the collective vision and aspirations of community members, city leaders, and local stakeholders.

Developed in partnership with RDG Planning & Design, the draft plan is now available for public review. The planning process included months of collaboration with City staff, private businesses, and the broader Muscatine community.

**The plan has three primary goals:**

*   Provide a legal foundation for future land use and development decisions;
*   Capture a clear and compelling vision for Muscatine, shaped by community input;
*   Outline policies and actions needed to turn that vision into reality.

**Four key themes guided development of the plan:**

*   **Make it Ambitious** – Inspire future progress and innovation;
*   **Make it Home** – Expand and enhance housing opportunities for all residents;
*   **Make it Connected** – Create a cohesive, multi-modal transportation network;
*   **Make it Adventurous** – Elevate recreation and outdoor amenities citywide.

The public is invited to review the draft plan and share input through the project website, [**Make It Muscatine**](http://muscatineiowa.gov/%22https://rdgusa.mysocialpinpoint.com/planmuscatine/plan-muscatine-page-1/%22). The site includes the full draft, an interactive map for sharing ideas, event updates, and background information on the planning process.

**Public Engagement Highlights:**

*   A technical committee of City staff and consultants began meeting in early 2024.
*   A diverse steering committee, including public and private representatives, guided planning efforts.
*   A Community Roundtable was held October 15, 2024, inviting residents to define priorities and aspirations.
*   Stakeholder interviews and a project website launch followed in Fall 2024.
*   A public Design Studio held on January 22, 2025, allowed participants to shape draft concepts.

The City and RDG Planning & Design are currently incorporating feedback into the final draft. A public open house will be scheduled soon, offering another opportunity for residents to review the plan and help prioritize future initiatives before final adoption.

Comments on the draft plan may also be sent via the virtual comment box that is located at the following link: [Comment Box](http://muscatineiowa.gov/%22https://www.surveymonkey.com/r/muscatinevirtualcommentbox%22).

**Stay Involved:**

Bookmark the [**Make It Muscatine**](http://muscatineiowa.gov/%22https://rdgusa.mysocialpinpoint.com/planmuscatine/plan-muscatine-page-1/%22) website and check back often for updates and opportunities to participate. You can also find links to the Comprehensive Plan on the [City of Muscatine website](http://muscatineiowa.gov/%22https://www.muscatineiowa.gov/%22), under “Common Service Requests” or the Community Development page.

Let’s work together to shape Muscatine’s future — **Make it Muscatine.**

Muscatine officials address concerns over mall, following the loss of Younkers
==============================================================================

![Image 1](https://gray-kwqc-prod.gtv-cdn.com/resizer/v2/P5FGGEPPWZJHJPCTQZ7K3JTIGQ.jpg?auth=0ddc3dad93a14e038f9d47d10c73f02823a60f25131dd46d1007267615e86dcb&width=800&height=450&smart=true)

(KWQC)

By Terrace Myles

Published: Apr. 19, 2018 at 5:45 PM CDT

Following the announcement of all Younker's stores closing, the economic impact may be bigger in certain cities, specifically Muscatine.

The Muscatine mall has seen a few stores leave over the past few years, one of the more notable big stores to leave was JCPenney's, which closed in 2014.

Since the announcement was made that Younkers was closing too, many residents feel their options at the Muscatine mall are running thin.

"Muscatine doesn't really have that many options for buying clothes," said longtime Younker's customer, Diane Meyers. She like many other people spent time with loved ones at the retail store. "This has been a place where my mother and I spend a lot of time, we'd have coffee on Tuesday and after coffee, we'd always come out go shopping here."

But it's the convenience factor of Younkers, that's fading away quickly. "We have to go to Davenport, every time we need to get something whether it's shoe clothes we have to go all the way to Davenport or Iowa City," said Madalyn Wheeler.

That's a big economic scare for Muscatine, Muscatine Mayor Dianna Broderson says the mall has had limited options for quite some time - and that has frustrated

customers.

"Anytime you lose a big store like that the economic impact that the on a community that it serves is really felt," Broderson said. She says due to its unique location between Davenport and Iowa City, it has been a challenge to bring in big stores to the mall that people often depend on, she admits the mall does need something new to bring in customers.

"The city certainly has worked with the mall over the years to try to revitalize it and efforts continue," she said.

One of the most recognizable names in Iowa retail will be gone by the end of the summer.

The sale of Younkers' parent company Bon-Ton Stores Inc. to a liquidation company awaits a Delaware bankruptcy judge's signature to finalize the deal.

![Image 2: Rhonda Thomas of Des Moines shops for some good deals at Younkers at Southridge Mall in Des Moines in 2012.](https://www.desmoinesregister.com/story/money/business/2018/04/18/younkers-bon-ton-close-sale-bankruptcy-stores-iowa-shopping-retail-amazon-going-out-business/528308002/)

Under the agreement, the company's 256 stores, including 49 Younkers stores, will close by the end of August and assets, including store merchandise and property, will be sold.

Bon-Ton Stores Inc., the owner of Younkers has filed for bankruptcy which could lead to the closure of the company's 250 stores, including 15 in Iowa.](https://www.desmoinesregister.com/story/money/business/2018/04/18/younkers-bon-ton-close-sale-bankruptcy-stores-iowa-shopping-retail-amazon-going-out-business/528308002/)

It's the end of an era for Iowa shoppers used to seeing the Younkers name on shopping malls across the state. The company was founded in Keokuk in 1856 and grew to become the largest department store chain in Iowa and Nebraska.

There are 17 Younkers stores remaining in Iowa that will close with the liquidation.

**More:** [What Iowa shoppers are saying about the Younkers closure on social media](https://www.desmoinesregister.com/story/news/local/2018/04/18/younkers-close-iowa-memories-thoughts-twitter-facebook-social-media-posts/527739002/)

Great American Group and Tiger Capital Group reportedly reached an agreement to purchase Bon-Ton for $775.5 million on Tuesday, according to the website Reorg Research.

A hearing was scheduled for Wednesday afternoon for the judge to sign off on the agreement terms, which would close all Bon-Ton stores by Aug. 31.

[![Image 4](https://www.desmoinesregister.com/story/money/business/2018/04/18/younkers-bon-ton-close-sale-bankruptcy-stores-iowa-shopping-retail-amazon-going-out-business/528308002/)](https://www.desmoinesregister.com/picture-gallery/news/local/des-moines/2014/03/29/the-younkers-building-the-downtown-store-through-the-years/7050159/)According to bankruptcy filings, Bon-Ton operates stores in 23 states that employ about 23,000 people. The company owns 22 locations and leases the remaining.

It operates stores under the names Younkers, Bon-Ton, Carson Pirie, Herberger's, Bergner's, Boston Store and Elder-Beerman.

Bon-Ton is the latest in a string of big-box retailers to close.

Toys R Us is closing all its stores while Macy's, Sears and Kmart are cutting back significantly on locations. Retailers have blamed online shopping in part on the demise of the brick and mortar stores.

► More: [Younkers' parent company has filed for bankruptcy. What will happen to Des Moines stores?](https://www.desmoinesregister.com/story/money/business/2018/02/05/younkers-parent-company-bankruptcy-des-moines-stores-close/307279002/)

Locally, Younkers has stores at four Des Moines-area malls, including Merle Hay Mall, Southridge, Jordan Creek Town Center and Valley West Mall. How soon those locations could close has not yet been announced.

![Image 5: There are 17 Younkers stores in Iowa that will close by the end of the summer.](https://www.desmoinesregister.com/story/money/business/2018/04/18/younkers-bon-ton-close-sale-bankruptcy-stores-iowa-shopping-retail-amazon-going-out-business/528308002/)

And what does the Bon-Ton demise portend for department stores in general?

"This is not the end of department stores," said Richard Hurd, a longtime retail developer in the Des Moines area. "I think we'll see a continuation of a pruning, not an end. Some strong players in the high-end and middle- to high-end category will continue to thrive and be dominate."

But echoing the sentiments of hundreds of longtime Younkers shoppers, Hurd said closing the stores is a loss for the community.

"This is a big loss," he said. "It's part of our heritage here in Iowa. Anyone in their late 20s, early 30s and older, I think, has a warm place in their heart for Younkers."

The liquidation company's sale agreement outlines some of the rules for the liquidation sale, including:

*   Returns to be made 10 days from the start of the sale.
*   Gift cards and credits to be used within 10 days from the sale start.
*   Liquidation company can add outside items to the sale if they are similar to the stores' merchandise.
*   The company will continue online sales for four weeks.
*   Some current employees may be kept on to work at the liquidation sale.

Accidents happen when you are living on and enjoying furniture in your home. With our furniture protection plans, you don’t need to worry about accidental damage. Protect against tears, scrapes, and breaks for up to five years after purchase! Help is always just a call away.

We look forward to serving you!

[### Muscatine Mall](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Muscatine_Mall)Shopping mall in Muscatine, Iowa, USMuscatine Mall, originally Muscatine Plaza, is a shopping mall in Muscatine, Iowa, United States. Its anchor stores are the Lab, Slumberland Furniture, and Warehouse Bargains. Built in 1971 by General Management, the mall originally featured Woolworth and Montgomery Ward as its anchor stores, with JCPenney joining in 1975. Woolworth was converted to Woolco, which closed in 1983 and became the first Walmart in the state of Iowa. After Walmart moved to a larger store, their space became Menards, which also relocated and was replaced by Slumberland Furniture. Montgomery Ward became Von Maur, Staples, Elder-Beerman, Younkers, and Compton's Furniture & More before becoming Warehouse Bargains. The mall has undergone a number of periods of decline, owing to relocation and closure of charter tenants. It is owned and managed by Muscatine Mall Management, LLC.

Mall bought by chain
====================

[Arlene Birt](https://iowastatedaily.com/staff_name/arlene-birt/)  
August 24, 1998

Ames’ North Grand Mall is one of five Iowa shopping malls going through a change of management due to an August buyout. The 351,000 square-foot mall, formerly owned by Teacher’s Insurance and Annuity Association (TIAA) and Rouse Companies, was purchased by Landau and Heyman.

Landau and Heyman is a 65-year-old retail real estate development company based in Chicago.

“Landau and Heyman’s strategic objective is to provide quality shopping in under-served markets,” said Gerry Curciarello, managing director and chief financial officer for Landau and Heyman, in a recent press release.

“By acquiring these five centers, which collectively have some real upside potential, we have an opportunity to add value and strengthen each center’s position in the marketplace,” he added.

Though Landau and Heyman has not yet announced any significant changes in the way North Grand Mall, 2801 Grand Ave., is managed or leased, store managers hope the mall will continue to run the same.

“I am hoping no changes will be made,” said Sheryl Ford, manager of Seiferts. “\[TIAA and Rouse Co.\] had been doing a good job at keeping the mall 100 percent leased.”

The only difference many managers have noticed so far is the change in address where lease payments are sent.

Fox Jewelry Co. Inc. manager Eric Hanson said he has heard only minor complaints, like the temperature of the mall is not kept cool enough in the summer.

“Though \[lowering the temperature\] may cost a lot more, if you draw people in to escape the heat, it would be worth it,” Hanson said.

Other Iowa malls included in the Landau and Heyman buyout are: Westland Mall in West Burlington, College Square Mall in Cedar Falls, Marshall Town Center in Marshalltown and Muscatine Mall in Muscatine.

Opened in 1971 as a twin. It was expanded to four screens on May 28, 1993. Of the three theatres that were once located in Muscatine this was the only one operating in 2013. It was operated by Fridley Theatres showing first run attractions.

It was closed by Fridlay Theatres on May 4, 2013, as they had opened their new 10-screen multiplex on March 14, 2013.
